cases.presentingComplaint: Yellow discolouration of skin and eyes noticed on day 3 of life

trapActions.explanation: ⚠️ Phenobarbitone is not first-line for neonatal jaundice — phototherapy is. Deducted −15 pts.
⚠️ Exchange transfusion requires checking serum bilirubin level and gestational age thresholds first. Deducted −15 pts.

hpc_onset.text: The yellow colour started on day 2 — we noticed the eyes first, then the skin turned yellow by day 3. He was born at term, normal vaginal delivery.
hpc_onset.label: Onset

hpc_character.text: The yellow colour started from the face and has spread to the chest. It hasn't reached the hands and feet yet.
hpc_character.label: Distribution

birth_history.text: Born at 39 weeks by SVD. Birth weight 3.2 kg. APGAR score was 8 and 9. No resuscitation needed. Discharged at 24 hours.
birth_history.label: Birth history

feeding_history.text: He is exclusively breastfeeding — latching well. He feeds every 2–3 hours. Urine output is good — 6 wet nappies today. Stool is yellow-green.
feeding_history.label: Feeding history

blood_group.text: Mother is blood group O positive. We don't know the baby's blood group yet.
blood_group.label: Blood group

fhx_general.text: No family history of jaundice or blood disorders. First child. Mother had no infections during pregnancy.
fhx_general.label: Family history

pmh_general.text: No previous illness. This is a new baby — born 3 days ago with no complications.
pmh_general.label: Perinatal history

sr_fever.text: No fever. He has been warm but his temperature is normal — 36.8°C axillary.
sr_fever.label: Fever

exam_general.text: General: Alert, active, crying vigorously. Jaundice: face, trunk — not palms or soles (Zone 2–3 Kramer). Weight today: 3.05 kg (5% weight loss from birth — acceptable). Temp 36.9°C. HR 148 bpm. RR 46/min.
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_skin.text: Skin: Jaundice visible on face and trunk. Blanching test confirms jaundice. No petechiae, no bruising. Umbilical stump: healthy, no infection.
exam_skin.label: Skin examination

exam_abdomen.text: Abdomen: Soft. Liver: 2cm below costal margin (normal for neonate). Spleen not palpable. No masses.
exam_abdomen.label: Abdominal examination

ix_bilirubin.text:
Serum Bilirubin (total): 185 μmol/L
• Indirect (unconjugated): 178 μmol/L ↑
• Direct (conjugated): 7 μmol/L (normal)
→ Predominantly unconjugated — consistent with physiological or haemolytic jaundice.
→ At day 3, term infant: phototherapy threshold ~220 μmol/L (NICE chart). Currently BELOW threshold.
ix_bilirubin.label: Serum bilirubin

ix_fbc.text:
FBC:
• Hb: 18.2 g/dL (normal for neonate)
• Reticulocytes: 3% (slightly raised)
• WBC: 12.4 × 10⁹/L (normal)
• Platelets: 280 × 10⁹/L
→ No significant haemolysis. No evidence of sepsis.
ix_fbc.label: FBC

ix_bloodgroup.text:
Baby's blood group: A positive
Direct Coombs Test (DCT): Negative
→ No ABO/Rh incompatibility. G6PD screen: pending.
ix_bloodgroup.label: Blood group & Coombs

cases.presentingComplaint: Failure to thrive and bilateral leg swelling for 6 weeks

trapActions.explanation: ⛔ High protein feeding in kwashiorkor causes refeeding syndrome. WHO F-75 (low protein) is given first. Deducted −20 pts.
⛔ Diuretics are contraindicated in oedematous malnutrition — they worsen electrolyte imbalance and cause circulatory collapse. Deducted −15 pts.
⛔ Rapid IV fluids in SAM cause fatal cardiac overload. Use oral/NG ReSoMal only unless in shock. Deducted −20 pts.

hpc_onset.text: (Mother) She stopped growing about 2 months ago. The leg swelling started 6 weeks ago and has been getting worse. She used to walk well but now she's weak.
hpc_onset.label: Onset

feeding_history.text: (Mother) I stopped breastfeeding at 12 months when I got pregnant again. She mostly eats ogi (pap) and sometimes rice. We can't always afford meat or fish.
feeding_history.label: Feeding history

hpc_character.text: (Mother) Her whole body looks swollen — the legs the most. Her face is also puffy. She has hair that keeps falling out and her skin has patches.
hpc_character.label: Clinical features

sr_diarrhoea.text: (Mother) Yes, she has had watery diarrhoea for 3 days. About 4–5 times per day. Sometimes with mucus.
sr_diarrhoea.label: Diarrhoea

sr_fever.text: (Mother) She felt warm 2 days ago. I didn't check the temperature. She seems cold today actually.
sr_fever.label: Fever

immunisation.text: (Mother) She had her baby vaccines but I missed some at 9 months because we moved. I'm not sure she got measles vaccine.
immunisation.label: Immunisation

pmh_general.text: (Mother) She has had malaria twice. No hospital admissions. No known chronic illness.
pmh_general.label: Past medical history

shx_general.text: (Mother) We are five children in the house. Father is a farmer — income is poor. We live in a single room in a rural community outside Zaria.
shx_general.label: Social history

exam_general.text: General: Apathetic, not crying. Oedema: bilateral pitting oedema feet and legs (2+). Face: moon face, oedematous. Hair: reddish, sparse, easily pluckable. Skin: flaky paint dermatosis — hyperpigmented and hypopigmented patches. Temp 35.8°C (hypothermia). HR 96 bpm. RR 40/min. SpO₂ 96%.
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_muac.text:
MUAC: 10.8 cm (< 11.5 cm = SAM threshold)
Weight: 7.2 kg (Expected for age 2F: ~12 kg → severely underweight)
Height: 78 cm
WHZ score: −3.8 SD (severe wasting)
→ Meets SAM criteria on both MUAC and WHZ.
exam_muac.label: Anthropometry

exam_abdomen.text: Abdomen: Distended. Liver palpable 4cm below costal margin. No ascites clinically. Bowel sounds present.
exam_abdomen.label: Abdominal examination

ix_fbc.text:
FBC:
• Hb: 7.2 g/dL ↓↓ (severe anaemia)
• WBC: 6.8 × 10⁹/L (low-normal — immune suppression common in SAM)
• Platelets: 110 × 10⁹/L ↓
→ Severe anaemia — do NOT transfuse unless Hb < 4 g/dL or cardiac signs (risk of overload).
ix_fbc.label: FBC

ix_glucose.text:
Blood glucose: 2.8 mmol/L ↓ (hypoglycaemia — SAM emergency)
→ Give 10% dextrose 5ml/kg stat orally or NG. Recheck in 30 minutes.
ix_glucose.label: Blood glucose

ix_lft.text:
Electrolytes:
• Na: 128 mmol/L ↓ (hyponatraemia)
• K: 2.9 mmol/L ↓↓ (hypokalaemia)
• Albumin: 14 g/L ↓↓ (severe hypoalbuminaemia — explains oedema)
→ Correct electrolytes cautiously. Potassium supplementation essential.
ix_lft.label: Electrolytes / Albumin

cases.presentingComplaint: Fever, neck stiffness and altered consciousness for 1 day

trapActions.explanation: ⛔ LP is contraindicated with signs of raised ICP (papilloedema, coning posture). Do NOT perform LP first. Deducted −20 pts.
⛔ Antibiotics must NOT be delayed waiting for LP or cultures in suspected bacterial meningitis. Every hour counts. Deducted −20 pts.
⛔ Aspirin is contraindicated in children — Reye's syndrome risk. Deducted −20 pts.

hpc_onset.text: (Mother) He was well yesterday morning then developed high fever in the afternoon. By evening he was very irritable. This morning he couldn't move his neck and wasn't recognising me.
hpc_onset.label: Onset

sr_fever.text: (Mother) Very high fever — 40.1°C. It's been there since yesterday. Paracetamol helped a little but it came back.
sr_fever.label: Fever

sr_seizures.text: (Mother) Yes! He had a fit this morning — both arms and legs shaking for about 4 minutes. He was unconscious after.
sr_seizures.label: Seizures

sr_consciousness.text: (Mother) He's very drowsy — he only opens his eyes when I call him loudly. He's not responding normally. He's not talking.
sr_consciousness.label: Consciousness

sr_rash.text: (Mother) I noticed some small red spots on his legs this morning. I thought it was just mosquito bites at first.
sr_rash.label: Rash

hpc_character.text: (Mother) He screams when I pick him up — as if being touched hurts him. He's been pulling at his head.
hpc_character.label: Irritability / photophobia

immunisation.text: (Mother) He received his EPI vaccines. I'm not sure he received the meningococcal vaccine — we missed some visits.
immunisation.label: Immunisation

pmh_general.text: (Mother) He had pneumonia last year and was admitted for 5 days. Otherwise healthy. No other conditions.
pmh_general.label: Past medical history

exam_general.text: General: Drowsy, irritable when disturbed. GCS 10/15 (E3V3M4). Temp 40.2°C. HR 148 bpm. BP 88/56 mmHg ↓. RR 44/min. SpO₂ 95%. Ill-looking, toxic appearance.
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_neuro.text: Neuro: Neck rigidity ++ (positive Brudzinski). Kernig's sign: positive bilaterally. Pupils 4mm equal and reactive. Fontanelle: closed (age 3 — normal). No papilloedema on fundoscopy. Tone normal.
exam_neuro.label: Neurological examination

exam_skin.text:
Skin: Non-blanching petechiae on both lower limbs and trunk — 8–10 lesions, 1–3mm diameter.
→ NON-BLANCHING RASH = meningococcal septicaemia until proven otherwise. EMERGENCY.
exam_skin.label: Skin / rash

ix_lft.text:
Bloods:
• Na: 126 mmol/L ↓ (hyponatraemia — SIADH in meningitis)
• Glucose: 3.1 mmol/L
• WBC: 22.4 × 10⁹/L ↑↑ (neutrophilia)
• CRP: 186 mg/L ↑↑
• Blood cultures: sent — results pending
ix_lft.label: Bloods / cultures

ix_csf.text:
CSF (performed after stabilisation, no papilloedema):
• Appearance: turbid/cloudy
• WBC: 2400 cells/μL (predominantly neutrophils 92%)
• Protein: 3.8 g/L ↑↑ (normal <0.4)
• Glucose: 0.8 mmol/L ↓ (CSF:blood ratio 0.26 — very low)
• Gram stain: Gram-negative diplococci
→ Bacterial (meningococcal) meningitis confirmed.
ix_csf.label: CSF analysis

cases.presentingComplaint: Severe pain in arms, legs and back for 2 days

trapActions.explanation: ⛔ Aspirin is contraindicated in children — Reye's syndrome risk. Deducted −20 pts.
⚠️ NSAIDs should be used cautiously in SCD — risk of renal impairment. Use paracetamol and opioids for acute crisis. Deducted −15 pts.
⛔ Fluid restriction worsens sickling. Patients in crisis need good hydration — at least 1.5× maintenance. Deducted −20 pts.

hpc_onset.text: The pain started 2 days ago. It was in my legs first, then spread to my arms and back. It came on gradually after we had very cold weather.
hpc_onset.label: Onset & trigger

hpc_character.text: It's a very deep, boring pain — like something is crushing my bones. I can't sleep or walk properly. It's the worst pain I've had.
hpc_character.label: Pain character

hpc_triggers.text: Cold weather and getting dehydrated make my crises worse. I didn't drink enough water at school the day before this started.
hpc_triggers.label: Precipitating factors

pmh_general.text: I have sickle cell disease — HbSS. I've had about 4 crises in the last year. I was admitted last year with acute chest syndrome.
pmh_general.label: SCD history

meds_general.text: I take folic acid daily and penicillin V twice a day. I was taking hydroxyurea but we ran out 2 months ago and couldn't get more.
meds_general.label: Medications

sr_fever.text: I feel warm. My mum checked — 38.5°C. I'm not sure if it's from pain or infection.
sr_fever.label: Fever

sr_chest.text: There's no chest pain right now. I'm breathing okay. But I had acute chest last year — I know what that feels like.
sr_chest.label: Chest symptoms

fhx_general.text: Both my parents carry the sickle cell trait (AS). My older sister also has SS disease.
fhx_general.label: Family history

exam_general.text: General: In significant pain, grimacing. Temp 38.6°C. HR 116 bpm. BP 104/68. RR 22/min. SpO₂ 97% on air. Pallor + (mild, chronic). Mild scleral icterus (chronic haemolysis).
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_abdomen.text: Abdomen: Spleen not palpable (autosplenectomy by age 9 — typical in HbSS). Liver: 2cm below costal margin. No tenderness. No splenic sequestration.
exam_abdomen.label: Abdominal examination

exam_msk.text: Musculoskeletal: Bilateral tenderness over humeri and tibiae. No joint swelling or warmth. No bony deformity. Full range of movement limited by pain.
exam_msk.label: Musculoskeletal examination

ix_fbc.text:
FBC:
• Hb: 7.1 g/dL (baseline for this patient is ~7–8 g/dL)
• Reticulocytes: 8% ↑ (haemolysis)
• WBC: 18.2 × 10⁹/L ↑ (common in SCD crisis even without infection)
• Platelets: 430 × 10⁹/L ↑
→ Hb at baseline — no acute haemolysis. Leukocytosis — may reflect crisis (not necessarily sepsis).
ix_fbc.label: FBC

ix_lft.text:
Metabolic:
• Na: 136 mmol/L
• Creatinine: 68 μmol/L (normal)
• Bilirubin: 52 μmol/L ↑ (unconjugated — ongoing haemolysis)
• LDH: 640 IU/L ↑ (haemolysis marker)
→ No acute organ damage. Hydration adequate.
ix_lft.label: Metabolic panel

cases.presentingComplaint: Convulsion lasting 3 minutes associated with fever

trapActions.explanation: ⛔ Aspirin is contraindicated in children — Reye's syndrome. Deducted −20 pts.
⚠️ Long-term anticonvulsants are NOT indicated for simple febrile convulsions. Deducted −15 pts.

hpc_onset.text: (Mother) She had high fever since this morning. About 2 hours after the fever started, she suddenly stiffened, then started shaking all over — arms and legs.
hpc_onset.label: Onset

hpc_character.text: (Mother) The shaking lasted about 3 minutes. It involved both arms and legs. Her eyes rolled upward. She was unconscious during it but woke up after — confused for a few minutes then okay.
hpc_character.label: Seizure description

sr_fever.text: (Mother) Temperature was 39.4°C when I checked before coming. I gave paracetamol syrup before coming to the hospital.
sr_fever.label: Fever

sr_consciousness.text: (Mother) She cried and was confused for about 5 minutes after the fit but now she's alert and recognising me normally.
sr_consciousness.label: Post-ictal state

pmh_general.text: (Mother) She had one febrile convulsion before at age 18 months — same thing, short fit with fever. No epilepsy diagnosis. Development is normal.
pmh_general.label: Previous febrile seizures

fhx_general.text: (Mother) My brother had febrile convulsions as a child — he grew out of them. No epilepsy in the family.
fhx_general.label: Family history

sr_urt.text: (Mother) She's had a runny nose and cough for 2 days. I think she has a cold.
sr_urt.label: Source of fever

immunisation.text: (Mother) She is up to date on all vaccines. She received her 9-month measles vaccine.
immunisation.label: Immunisation

exam_general.text: General: Alert, consolable, sitting on mother's lap. Temp 39.1°C (post-paracetamol). HR 134 bpm. RR 36/min. SpO₂ 99%. No respiratory distress. Pink, well-perfused.
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_neuro.text: Neuro: GCS 15. Alert, appropriate, follows commands. Pupils equal and reactive. No neck stiffness. No Kernig's. Fontanelle: closed (normal for age 2). Tone, reflexes normal. No focal deficit.
exam_neuro.label: Neurological examination

exam_throat.text: ENT: Throat: red, inflamed tonsils. Cervical lymph nodes: mildly tender. TMs: clear. Chest: clear, no wheeze or crackles. Runny nose — clear discharge.
exam_throat.label: ENT / Throat

ix_glucose.text:
Blood glucose: 5.2 mmol/L (normal)
→ Hypoglycaemia excluded as cause of seizure.
ix_glucose.label: Blood glucose

ix_fbc.text:
FBC:
• WBC: 13.8 × 10⁹/L (mild lymphocytosis — viral pattern)
• Hb: 11.2 g/dL
→ Viral URTI likely source of fever. No bacterial infection pattern.
ix_fbc.label: FBC

cases.presentingComplaint: Cough, fast breathing and fever for 4 days

trapActions.explanation: ⚠️ Antivirals are not routinely indicated for bacterial pneumonia. Antibiotics are the treatment. Deducted −10 pts.
⚠️ Aminoglycosides alone are not first-line for CAP in children. Amoxicillin/ampicillin is first-line. Deducted −15 pts.

hpc_onset.text: (Mother) He started with a runny nose 5 days ago, then developed cough and fever 4 days ago. The breathing has become very fast since yesterday.
hpc_onset.label: Onset

hpc_character.text: (Mother) He's been coughing a lot — productive cough with yellowish-green phlegm. Breathing very fast and he's using extra muscles to breathe — I can see his ribs.
hpc_character.label: Cough & breathing

sr_fever.text: (Mother) High fever — 39°C. It's been there for 4 days. Paracetamol helps temporarily but it keeps coming back.
sr_fever.label: Fever

sr_feeding.text: (Mother) He has been eating much less than normal — only took half a cup of rice today. He's drinking, but less than usual.
sr_feeding.label: Feeding / appetite

pmh_general.text: (Mother) He had malaria 3 months ago. No asthma, no previous hospital admission for breathing. No TB contacts that I know of.
pmh_general.label: Past medical history

immunisation.text: (Mother) He is fully vaccinated — including pneumococcal (PCV) at the right times.
immunisation.label: Immunisation

shx_general.text: (Mother) Lives with parents and 3 siblings. Father smokes indoors. We use a kerosene stove for cooking — the kitchen is inside the house.
shx_general.label: Social & environmental history

exam_general.text: General: Ill-looking, tachypnoeic. Temp 39.2°C. HR 128 bpm. RR 52/min ↑↑ (WHO fast breathing threshold for age 5: ≥40/min). SpO₂ 93% on air ↓. Nasal flaring present. Subcostal recession present.
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_chest.text:
Chest:
• Inspection: increased respiratory rate, subcostal recession, nasal flaring
• Percussion: dull at right lower zone
• Auscultation: reduced breath sounds right lower zone, fine inspiratory crackles right base, bronchial breath sounds right lower lobe
→ Consolidation right lower lobe.
exam_chest.label: Chest examination

ix_cxr.text:
CXR:
• Right lower lobe consolidation — homogeneous opacity
• Air bronchograms visible
• No pleural effusion
• No pneumothorax
→ Consistent with right lower lobe bacterial pneumonia.
ix_cxr.label: Chest X-ray

ix_fbc.text:
FBC:
• WBC: 19.4 × 10⁹/L ↑↑ (neutrophilia 16.2 × 10⁹/L)
• CRP: 112 mg/L ↑↑
• Hb: 10.8 g/dL (mild anaemia)
→ Bacterial infection pattern confirmed.
ix_fbc.label: FBC / CRP

cases.presentingComplaint: Vomiting, deep breathing and drowsiness in a known diabetic

trapActions.explanation: ⛔ Rapid fluid boluses in paediatric DKA increase cerebral oedema risk. Use slow rehydration over 48 hours per DKA protocol. Deducted −20 pts.
⚠️ Sodium bicarbonate is NOT recommended in DKA — it worsens cerebral oedema and paradoxical CSF acidosis. Deducted −15 pts.
⛔ IV fluids must be started BEFORE insulin in DKA. Starting insulin without adequate hydration causes severe hypokalaemia. Deducted −20 pts.

hpc_onset.text: I've been feeling unwell for 3 days. Started with increased thirst and frequent urination, then vomiting since yesterday. My mum noticed I was breathing very deeply this morning.
hpc_onset.label: Onset

hpc_character.text: I feel very weak and drowsy. I vomited 6 times today and couldn't keep any fluids down. My stomach hurts. My mum said my breath smells fruity.
hpc_character.label: Symptoms

pmh_general.text: I've had Type 1 diabetes for 3 years. I use insulin — 24 units of glargine at night and a bolus before meals.
pmh_general.label: Diabetes history

meds_general.text: I ran out of insulin 4 days ago and we didn't get to refill it. I haven't taken any insulin in 4 days.
meds_general.label: Insulin compliance

sr_polyuria.text: Yes — I've been going to the toilet every 30–60 minutes, even at night. And drinking so much water but still thirsty.
sr_polyuria.label: Polyuria/polydipsia

sr_fever.text: No fever. I don't think I have an infection — but my chest feels a bit sore from vomiting.
sr_fever.label: Fever / infection screen

exam_general.text: General: Drowsy but rousable. GCS 13. Kussmaul breathing (deep, sighing respirations). Fruity (acetone) breath detectable. Temp 37.0°C. HR 124 bpm. BP 96/62 ↓. RR 32/min (deep). SpO₂ 99%. Severely dehydrated — sunken eyes, reduced skin turgor, dry mucous membranes. Weight 38 kg.
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_abdomen.text:
Abdomen: Generalised tenderness — diffuse, soft. No guarding or rigidity. Bowel sounds reduced. No organomegaly.
→ Abdominal pain is common in DKA and usually resolves with treatment.
exam_abdomen.label: Abdominal examination

ix_glucose.text:
Blood glucose: 28.4 mmol/L ↑↑ (hyperglycaemia)
Bedside ketones: 4.8 mmol/L ↑↑ (>3.0 = DKA)
→ DKA confirmed biochemically.
ix_glucose.label: Glucose & ketones

ix_abg.text:
Blood Gas (venous):
• pH: 7.11 ↓↓ (severe acidosis)
• HCO₃: 8 mmol/L ↓↓
• pCO₂: 2.4 kPa ↓ (respiratory compensation)
• Anion gap: 26 mEq/L ↑ (high AG metabolic acidosis)
→ Severe DKA (pH < 7.1, HCO₃ < 10).
ix_abg.label: Blood gas

ix_lft.text:
Electrolytes:
• Na: 131 mmol/L ↓ (corrected Na = 135 — adjust for hyperglycaemia)
• K: 3.1 mmol/L ↓ (CRITICAL — will fall further with insulin. Replace before starting insulin if K < 3.5)
• Creatinine: 102 μmol/L ↑ (pre-renal AKI — dehydration)
• HbA1c: 12.8% (very poorly controlled)
ix_lft.label: Electrolytes

cases.presentingComplaint: Mother brings 6-week-old for scheduled immunisation — child appears well

trapActions.explanation: ⚠️ BCG is given at birth — NOT repeated at 6 weeks. Repeating it is incorrect. Deducted −15 pts.
⚠️ Vaccines should not be given to acutely ill children with moderate-to-severe illness. Check the child first. Deducted −15 pts.

birth_vaccines.text: (Mother) She received BCG and OPV at birth in the hospital. The card shows both were given on day 1.
birth_vaccines.label: Birth vaccines

feeding_history.text: (Mother) She's exclusively breastfeeding — feeding every 2–3 hours. She's gaining weight well. No problems so far.
feeding_history.label: Feeding history

sr_fever.text: (Mother) No fever. She's been well since birth — no illness, no hospital visits.
sr_fever.label: Current health

pmh_general.text: (Mother) Normal pregnancy and delivery. Born at 39 weeks. Birth weight 3.1 kg. APGAR 9/10. Discharged day 2. No neonatal illness.
pmh_general.label: Birth history

allergies_general.text: (Mother) No known allergies. No adverse reactions to the birth vaccines.
allergies_general.label: Allergy screen

exam_general.text: General: Alert, active, feeding well. Weight: 4.6 kg (appropriate weight gain — +1.5 kg since birth over 6 weeks). Length: 55 cm. HC: 38 cm. Temp: 36.7°C. No jaundice. Umbilical stump healed. BCG scar visible at left deltoid.
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_neuro.text:
Developmental screen at 6 weeks:
• Social smile: present ✅
• Tracks horizontally: yes ✅
• Moro reflex: present ✅
• Grasp reflex: present ✅
→ Development appropriate for age.
exam_neuro.label: Developmental screen

ix_epi_schedule.text:
Nigerian EPI Schedule — 6-week vaccines due:
• Penta 1 (DTP + Hib + HepB) — IM right thigh
• OPV 1 — oral 2 drops
• PCV 1 (Pneumococcal) — IM left thigh
• Rotavirus 1 — oral

NOT due today: BCG (given at birth), IPV (14 weeks), MCV (9 months)
ix_epi_schedule.label: EPI schedule

counselling.text:
Counselled mother on:
• Expected side effects: mild fever and injection site swelling (normal for 24–48h)
• When to return: next visit at 10 weeks (Penta 2, OPV 2, PCV 2, Rota 2)
• Danger signs: high fever >39°C, inconsolable crying, fits — return immediately
• Exclusive breastfeeding until 6 months
counselling.label: Counselling given

cases.presentingComplaint: 5-day-old neonate — poor feeding, lethargy and fast breathing since yesterday

trapActions.explanation: ⛔ Chloramphenicol causes Grey Baby Syndrome in neonates — cardiovascular collapse. Absolutely contraindicated. Deducted −20 pts.
⛔ Tetracyclines are contraindicated in neonates — cause tooth discolouration and liver toxicity. Deducted −20 pts.
⚠️ Ceftriaxone is generally avoided in neonates — displaces bilirubin and causes hyperbilirubinaemia. Use cefotaxime instead. Deducted −15 pts.

hpc_onset.text: (Mother) He was feeding well the first 3 days. Yesterday he became very sleepy and refused the breast. This morning his breathing became very fast.
hpc_onset.label: Onset

birth_history.text: (Mother) Born at home by traditional birth attendant. 38 weeks. We cut the cord with a blade. Birth weight unknown. We came to hospital on day 2 when he seemed yellow.
birth_history.label: Birth history

feeding_history.text: (Mother) He was feeding every 3 hours before. Now he's too weak to suck. He took a few drops this morning and fell asleep.
feeding_history.label: Feeding changes

umbilical.text: (Mother) The cord stump looks a bit red and wet — I noticed it today. There's a little yellow discharge.
umbilical.label: Umbilical cord

maternal_history.text: (Mother) I had fever during labour — about 38.5°C. Labour lasted 20 hours. My membranes ruptured at home before the TBA arrived — maybe 18 hours before delivery.
maternal_history.label: Maternal risk factors

sr_fever.text: (Mother) He felt cold this morning — not warm. I'm worried because he looks pale.
sr_fever.label: Temperature instability

exam_general.text: General: Lethargic, floppy, poor tone. Does not cry when examined. Temp 35.2°C (hypothermia — common in neonatal sepsis). HR 178 bpm ↑↑. RR 72/min ↑↑. SpO₂ 90% on air. Pallor ++. Mild jaundice (Kramer Zone 3). Capillary refill: 4 seconds (poor perfusion).
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_umbilicus.text:
Umbilical stump: erythema extending 1cm onto abdominal skin (omphalitis). Purulent discharge present. Foul odour.
→ Omphalitis — portal of entry for neonatal sepsis.
exam_umbilicus.label: Umbilical examination

exam_chest.text:
Chest: Tachypnoea. Subcostal recession. Bilateral fine crepitations.
→ Neonatal pneumonia component likely.
exam_chest.label: Chest examination

ix_fbc.text:
FBC:
• WBC: 3.2 × 10⁹/L ↓ (leucopaenia — severe sepsis)
• Neutrophils: 1.1 × 10⁹/L ↓↓ (neutropaenia)
• I:T ratio: 0.38 ↑ (immature:total neutrophil ratio — indicates neonatal sepsis)
• Platelets: 68 × 10⁹/L ↓↓ (DIC risk)
• Hb: 12.4 g/dL
ix_fbc.label: FBC

ix_crp.text:
CRP: 148 mg/L ↑↑
Blood glucose: 1.8 mmol/L ↓ (hypoglycaemia — common in neonatal sepsis)
Blood cultures: sent — results awaited
→ Empirical antibiotics should NOT be delayed.
ix_crp.label: CRP / glucose / cultures

cases.presentingComplaint: Cough, wheeze and difficulty feeding for 3 days

trapActions.explanation: ⚠️ Salbutamol (bronchodilators) are NOT recommended for bronchiolitis — evidence shows no benefit. Deducted −10 pts.
⚠️ Antibiotics are not indicated for viral bronchiolitis unless secondary bacterial infection is suspected. Deducted −10 pts.
⚠️ Steroids are not recommended for bronchiolitis — no clinical benefit shown. Deducted −10 pts.

hpc_onset.text: (Mother) He had runny nose for 2 days, then developed cough and noisy breathing. The last 24 hours he's been struggling to feed — he gets breathless while feeding.
hpc_onset.label: Onset

feeding_history.text: (Mother) He normally takes a full breastfeed in 10 minutes. Now he pulls away after 2–3 minutes, breathless. He's taking less than half his normal amount.
feeding_history.label: Feeding difficulty

hpc_character.text: (Mother) He makes a whistling sound when he breathes — especially when breathing out. You can hear it without a stethoscope. His chest looks like it's working hard.
hpc_character.label: Wheeze / breathing

sr_fever.text: (Mother) Mild fever — 37.9°C. It came with the runny nose. No rigors.
sr_fever.label: Fever

pmh_general.text: (Mother) He was born at term. No previous breathing problems. No hospital admissions. No eczema.
pmh_general.label: Past medical history

fhx_general.text: (Mother) No family history of asthma. Father had eczema as a child.
fhx_general.label: Atopy history

shx_general.text: (Mother) Older sibling (age 4) had a cold last week and recovered. We live in a small flat — no cigarette smoke.
shx_general.label: Contact history

exam_general.text: General: Alert, tired-looking. Temp 37.8°C. HR 142 bpm. RR 58/min ↑↑. SpO₂ 92% on air ↓. Moderate subcostal and intercostal recession. Nasal flaring. No cyanosis.
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_chest.text:
Chest:
• Hyperinflated (increased AP diameter)
• Fine end-inspiratory crackles bilaterally
• High-pitched expiratory wheeze throughout
• Air entry: symmetrically reduced
→ Classic bronchiolitis picture: wheeze + crackles + hyperinflation.
exam_chest.label: Chest examination

ix_cxr.text:
CXR (if performed):
• Hyperinflation
• Peribronchial thickening
• Patchy atelectasis
→ CXR not routinely needed in typical bronchiolitis. Useful if diagnosis uncertain.
ix_cxr.label: CXR

ix_spo2_monitor.text:
SpO₂ monitoring: Baseline 92% → on 0.5L/min nasal cannula O₂: SpO₂ 96%
→ Requires supplemental oxygen. Admission indicated.
Feeding assessment: unable to complete full feed in 20 minutes → NG tube feeding indicated.
ix_spo2_monitor.label: SpO₂ & feeding assessment

cases.presentingComplaint: Prolonged fever, headache and abdominal pain for 10 days

trapActions.explanation: ⚠️ High rates of Salmonella resistance to ampicillin in Nigeria. Ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone is preferred. Deducted −15 pts.
⚠️ Chloramphenicol resistance is common in Nigeria. Fluoroquinolones or third-generation cephalosporins are now preferred. Deducted −10 pts.

hpc_onset.text: The fever started about 10 days ago. It was mild at first, then got worse. Headache started at the same time. Stomach pain started about 5 days ago.
hpc_onset.label: Onset & progression

hpc_character.text: The fever is there every day — it goes up in the evenings, comes down a little in the morning but never fully goes away. I feel very weak. I have dull pain all over my stomach.
hpc_character.label: Fever pattern

sr_diarrhoea.text: I had constipation for the first few days, now I have loose stools — 2–3 times a day. No blood in the stool.
sr_diarrhoea.label: Bowel symptoms

shx_general.text: We buy water from a tanker — we don't always boil it. I eat at the school canteen sometimes. My classmate was absent last week with similar fever.
shx_general.label: Water / food history

sr_rash.text: (Mother) I noticed 2–3 small pink spots on her tummy yesterday. I wasn't sure what they were.
sr_rash.label: Rose spots

pmh_general.text: No previous typhoid. No other chronic illnesses. Never admitted to hospital before.
pmh_general.label: Past medical history

meds_general.text: She took paracetamol and some herbs from the chemist. No antibiotics yet.
meds_general.label: Medications

exam_general.text: General: Ill, toxic-looking. Temp 39.6°C. HR 88 bpm (relative bradycardia for temperature — classic typhoid sign). RR 22/min. BP 100/62. Coated tongue. Mild jaundice. 3 salmon-pink macules on abdomen (rose spots).
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_abdomen.text: Abdomen: Soft. Liver: 3cm below costal margin (hepatomegaly). Spleen: 2cm palpable (splenomegaly). RIF tenderness — mild. Bowel sounds: hyperactive.
exam_abdomen.label: Abdominal examination

ix_fbc.text:
FBC:
• WBC: 3.4 × 10⁹/L ↓ (leucopaenia — hallmark of typhoid)
• Neutrophils: 1.8 × 10⁹/L ↓
• Platelets: 108 × 10⁹/L ↓
→ Leucopaenia + thrombocytopaenia = classic typhoid blood picture.
ix_fbc.label: FBC

ix_culture.text:
Blood Culture (Widal is unreliable — culture is gold standard):
→ Blood culture: Salmonella typhi grown (sensitivity pending)
→ Sensitivity: Resistant to ampicillin; Sensitive to ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone
→ Widal test: O antigen 1:160, H antigen 1:80 (supportive but not diagnostic)
ix_culture.label: Blood culture / Widal

cases.presentingComplaint: Sudden severe intermittent crying and drawing up of legs for 6 hours

trapActions.explanation: ⛔ Laxatives or purgatives are absolutely contraindicated in intussusception — risk of perforation. Deducted −20 pts.
⚠️ Intussusception is a surgical emergency — delay in diagnosis and treatment leads to bowel necrosis. Deducted −15 pts.

hpc_onset.text: (Mother) He was absolutely fine this morning — feeding and playing normally. Then 6 hours ago he suddenly started screaming and pulling his legs up to his tummy. It goes in waves — he screams for 2–3 minutes then stops completely, then screams again.
hpc_onset.label: Onset — colicky pattern

hpc_character.text: (Mother) Between the crying episodes he looks pale and very tired — almost limp. The episodes are getting more frequent. He vomited twice — first milk, then greenish fluid.
hpc_character.label: Episode description

sr_stool.text: (Mother) He passed one normal stool this morning. About 2 hours ago he passed something unusual — it looked like red jelly mixed with mucus. Very little of it.
sr_stool.label: Red currant jelly stool

feeding_history.text: (Mother) He has been exclusively breastfed. We started solids 3 weeks ago — pureed banana and pap. He was fine initially.
feeding_history.label: Feeding / weaning

pmh_general.text: (Mother) He was born at term, healthy, no problems since birth. He had rotavirus vaccine at 6 and 10 weeks.
pmh_general.label: Past medical history

sr_fever.text: (Mother) No fever at the start, but I think he feels warm now — he's been unwell for 6 hours.
sr_fever.label: Fever

exam_general.text: General: During episode — screaming, drawing legs up, face red. Between episodes — pale, lethargic, limp. Temp 37.8°C. HR 158 bpm. RR 44/min. Mild dehydration — dry lips. No jaundice.
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_abdomen.text:
Abdomen: Soft between episodes. RUQ: sausage-shaped mass palpable in right side — slightly tender. RIF: relatively empty (Dance's sign).
→ Sausage mass + Dance's sign = intussusception until proven otherwise.
exam_abdomen.label: Abdominal examination

exam_pr.text:
PR examination: Blood-stained mucus on gloved finger.
→ Red currant jelly on PR = classic intussusception sign.
exam_pr.label: Per-rectum examination

ix_ultrasound.text:
Abdominal USS:
• Target sign (bull's eye): concentric rings of bowel — DIAGNOSTIC for intussusception
• Location: ileo-colic junction
• No free fluid suggesting perforation
→ Confirms intussusception. Air enema reduction indicated urgently.
ix_ultrasound.label: Abdominal USS

ix_fbc.text:
FBC:
• WBC: 16.4 × 10⁹/L ↑ (stress response)
• Hb: 10.8 g/dL
AXR: Paucity of gas in RIF, small bowel dilatation
→ Partial bowel obstruction pattern.
ix_fbc.label: FBC / AXR

cases.presentingComplaint: Puffy face and swollen legs for 2 weeks

trapActions.explanation: ⚠️ Diuretics before steroids in nephrotic syndrome can worsen hypovolaemia and cause AKI. Steroids are first-line. Deducted −15 pts.
⚠️ Protein restriction is NOT recommended in nephrotic syndrome — patients lose protein and need adequate intake. Deducted −15 pts.

hpc_onset.text: (Mother) About 2 weeks ago she woke up with puffy eyes in the morning. I thought she was tired. Then her legs started swelling. By end of the day the swelling is worse.
hpc_onset.label: Onset

hpc_character.text: (Mother) The swelling is worse in the morning on the face, worse in the evening on the legs. She has put on weight — 2 kg in 2 weeks. Her tummy looks slightly bigger too.
hpc_character.label: Oedema pattern

sr_urine.text: (Mother) Her urine has been very foamy lately — very bubbly when she passes it. She's also passing much less urine than before.
sr_urine.label: Urine changes

sr_fever.text: (Mother) No fever. She seems well in herself — still going to school, eating fairly well.
sr_fever.label: Systemic symptoms

pmh_general.text: (Mother) She had a sore throat about 3 weeks ago — it settled without treatment. No other medical problems. Normal development.
pmh_general.label: Past medical history

fhx_general.text: (Mother) No family history of kidney disease or nephrotic syndrome that I know of.
fhx_general.label: Family history

exam_general.text: General: Well-looking, no distress. Periorbital puffiness (worse this morning). Temp 36.8°C. BP 100/62 mmHg (normal for age). HR 90 bpm. RR 22/min. Bilateral pitting oedema feet and ankles 2+. Weight: 22 kg (up 2 kg from school record 3 weeks ago).
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_abdomen.text: Abdomen: Mild ascites (shifting dullness present). No organomegaly. No tenderness.
exam_abdomen.label: Abdominal examination

ix_urinalysis.text:
Urinalysis:
• Protein: 4+ (massive proteinuria)
• Blood: trace
• Glucose: negative
24-hour urine protein: 3.8 g/day ↑↑ (>3.5g/day = nephrotic range in adults; >40mg/m²/hr in children)
ix_urinalysis.label: Urinalysis

ix_lft.text:
Bloods:
• Albumin: 16 g/L ↓↓ (severe hypoalbuminaemia — explains oedema)
• Total protein: 38 g/L ↓
• Cholesterol: 9.8 mmol/L ↑↑ (hypercholesterolaemia — classic tetrad)
• Creatinine: 58 μmol/L (normal renal function)
→ Nephrotic tetrad: massive proteinuria + hypoalbuminaemia + oedema + hyperlipidaemia.
ix_lft.label: Bloods / albumin

cases.presentingComplaint: Pallor, weakness and poor appetite for 6 weeks

trapActions.explanation: ⚠️ Blood transfusion is not indicated for mild-moderate iron deficiency anaemia without haemodynamic compromise. Oral iron therapy is first-line. Deducted −15 pts.
⚠️ Oral iron is first-line for IDA in children. IV iron is reserved for intolerance or malabsorption. Deducted −10 pts.

hpc_onset.text: (Mother) She has been looking pale for about 6 weeks. She gets tired easily — she used to run around but now she stops to rest. Her appetite has reduced.
hpc_onset.label: Onset

feeding_history.text: (Mother) She drinks a lot of cow's milk — maybe 5–6 cups a day. She doesn't eat much solid food because she always wants milk. She eats mostly pap and rice, rarely meat or vegetables.
feeding_history.label: Dietary history

sr_pica.text: (Mother) Yes — she eats soil sometimes when she's outside! And she chews on the wall paint. I keep stopping her but she does it again.
sr_pica.label: Pica

sr_diarrhoea.text: (Mother) No diarrhoea. Stool is normal — once a day.
sr_diarrhoea.label: GI symptoms

pmh_general.text: (Mother) She had malaria 4 months ago and was given treatment. No other illnesses. No hospital admissions.
pmh_general.label: Past medical history

deworm_history.text: (Mother) She has never been dewormed. She plays in the compound barefoot sometimes.
deworm_history.label: Deworming history

exam_general.text: General: Pale but alert. Temp 36.7°C. HR 122 bpm. RR 28/min. No respiratory distress. Pallor ++ (conjunctivae, palms, mucous membranes). No jaundice. No lymphadenopathy. Tongue: smooth and pale (atrophic glossitis).
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_cardiovascular.text: CVS: Tachycardia. Soft systolic flow murmur at apex (grade 2/6) — anaemia-related. No cardiac failure signs.
exam_cardiovascular.label: Cardiovascular examination

ix_fbc.text:
FBC:
• Hb: 6.8 g/dL ↓↓ (moderate anaemia)
• MCV: 62 fL ↓ (microcytic)
• MCH: 18 pg ↓ (hypochromic)
• WBC: 8.2 × 10⁹/L (normal)
• Platelets: 480 × 10⁹/L ↑ (reactive thrombocytosis common in IDA)
→ Microcytic hypochromic anaemia — consistent with IDA.
ix_fbc.label: FBC

ix_iron_studies.text:
Iron Studies:
• Serum iron: 4.2 μmol/L ↓ (low)
• TIBC: 98 μmol/L ↑ (raised)
• Ferritin: 4 ng/mL ↓↓ (severely depleted iron stores)
• Transferrin saturation: 4% ↓
→ Confirms iron deficiency. Stool for O&P: hookworm ova found.
ix_iron_studies.label: Iron studies

cases.presentingComplaint: Sudden high fever, non-blanching rash and deteriorating consciousness

trapActions.explanation: ⛔ NEVER delay antibiotics in suspected meningococcal disease for cultures. Give IV ceftriaxone IMMEDIATELY. Every minute counts — mortality doubles with each hour of delay. Deducted −25 pts.
⛔ LP is CONTRAINDICATED in haemodynamic instability. Stabilise first, give antibiotics, then consider LP. Deducted −20 pts.

hpc_onset.text: (Father, panicked) He was completely well this morning — playing normally. 8 hours ago he developed high fever and became very irritable. 3 hours ago the rash appeared and he's been getting worse fast.
hpc_onset.label: Rapid deterioration

sr_rash.text: (Father) The rash started as a few spots on his legs — I thought it was mosquito bites. But they spread quickly to his trunk and some are now dark-red, large blotches.
sr_rash.label: Rash progression

sr_consciousness.text: (Father) He recognised me 3 hours ago but now he's very hard to wake. He just groans when I shake him.
sr_consciousness.label: Deteriorating consciousness

sr_fever.text: (Father) Very high fever — I didn't check the temperature at home. He was shaking at first, then stopped.
sr_fever.label: Fever

immunisation.text: (Father) He had some vaccines as a baby. I'm not sure about meningococcal vaccine — we may have missed that one.
immunisation.label: Immunisation

pmh_general.text: (Father) Completely healthy child. No previous admissions. No chronic illness.
pmh_general.label: Past medical history

exam_general.text: General: CRITICALLY ILL. GCS 8/15 (E2V2M4). Temp 40.4°C. HR 178 bpm ↑↑. BP 72/40 mmHg ↓↓ (shock). RR 52/min ↑↑. SpO₂ 88% on air ↓↓. CRT: 6 seconds. Cold peripheries. Mottled skin.
exam_general.label: General — critical assessment

exam_skin.text:
Skin: Widespread non-blanching purpuric rash — trunk, limbs, face. Multiple stellate (star-shaped) lesions up to 2cm. Central necrotic areas developing on several lesions.
→ PURPURA FULMINANS — DIC in progress. This is a medical emergency.
exam_skin.label: Skin — purpura fulminans

exam_neuro.text:
Neuro: GCS 8. Does not follow commands. Pupils 4mm, sluggish reaction. Neck: mild stiffness.
→ Meningococcal meningitis + septicaemia.
exam_neuro.label: Neurological examination

ix_fbc.text:
FBC (emergency):
• WBC: 2.1 × 10⁹/L ↓↓ (leucopaenia — overwhelming sepsis)
• Platelets: 24 × 10⁹/L ↓↓↓ (DIC)
• Hb: 8.4 g/dL ↓
Coagulation:
• PT: 32 sec ↑↑, APTT: 68 sec ↑↑
• Fibrinogen: 0.8 g/L ↓↓ (DIC confirmed)
ix_fbc.label: FBC / coagulation — DIC

ix_culture.text:
Blood cultures: sent (do NOT delay antibiotics for this)
Lactate: 8.4 mmol/L ↑↑↑ (severe septic shock)
Blood glucose: 1.6 mmol/L ↓ (hypoglycaemia — treat immediately)
→ IV ceftriaxone 80mg/kg STAT should already be running.
ix_culture.label: Cultures / lactate

cases.presentingComplaint: Unconscious child with high fever and repeated seizures

trapActions.explanation: ⚠️ IV artesunate is first-line for severe/cerebral malaria — NOT quinine. Artesunate reduces mortality by 35% vs quinine. Deducted −15 pts.
⛔ Chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum is endemic in Nigeria. NEVER use chloroquine for severe malaria. Deducted −20 pts.
⚠️ Corticosteroids are NOT recommended in cerebral malaria — trials showed increased mortality and complications. Deducted −15 pts.

hpc_onset.text: (Father) She had fever for 2 days — we thought it was malaria and gave her Coartem at home. Yesterday she started having fits. This morning she wouldn't wake up.
hpc_onset.label: Onset — self-treatment failure

sr_seizures.text: (Father) She had 3 fits at home — each one lasted 3–5 minutes. Full body shaking. She was unconscious between some of them. We panicked and brought her immediately.
sr_seizures.label: Seizures

sr_fever.text: (Father) Very high fever — 40°C at home. She was sweating a lot before the fits.
sr_fever.label: Fever

shx_travel.text: (Father) We live in a peri-urban area — there are many mosquitoes. She was bitten a lot last week after a rain storm. No travel elsewhere.
shx_travel.label: Exposure history

meds_general.text: (Father) We gave her 2 doses of Coartem (artemether-lumefantrine) at home yesterday — but she vomited after the second dose. She may not have absorbed it.
meds_general.label: Prior treatment

pmh_general.text: (Father) She had malaria twice before at ages 2 and 4 — treated successfully both times. No chronic illness. Up to date on vaccines.
pmh_general.label: Past medical history

exam_general.text: General: UNCONSCIOUS. Blantyre Coma Scale: 2/5 (eyes closed, doesn't localise pain, no verbal response — cerebral malaria confirmed by BCS ≤2). Temp 40.1°C. HR 162 bpm. BP 88/54 ↓. RR 46/min (irregular — Cheyne-Stokes pattern). SpO₂ 91%. Severe pallor.
exam_general.label: General — coma assessment

exam_neuro.text:
Neuro: BCS 2/5. Pupils: unequal — right 5mm sluggish, left 3mm reactive (herniation sign). Abnormal posturing — decerebrate on right.
→ SIGNS OF RAISED ICP — cerebral oedema likely.
exam_neuro.label: Neurological examination

exam_abdomen.text: Abdomen: Hepatosplenomegaly — liver 5cm, spleen 4cm below costal margins. No ascites.
exam_abdomen.label: Abdominal examination

ix_rdt.text:
Malaria RDT: P. falciparum POSITIVE
Blood film: Parasitaemia 6.2% (hyperparasitaemia >2% = severe malaria criterion)
Blood glucose: 1.4 mmol/L ↓↓ (HYPOGLYCAEMIA — treat immediately with IV dextrose)
→ IV artesunate 3mg/kg STAT indicated.
ix_rdt.label: Malaria / glucose

ix_fbc.text:
FBC:
• Hb: 4.8 g/dL ↓↓ (severe anaemia — transfusion threshold in cerebral malaria)
• Platelets: 34 × 10⁹/L ↓
• WBC: 11.8 × 10⁹/L
→ Severe anaemia meets WHO transfusion criteria (Hb < 5g/dL with respiratory distress).
ix_fbc.label: FBC

cases.presentingComplaint: Poor weight gain, fast breathing and sweating during feeds since birth

diagnosis.primary: Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) with Heart Failure

trapActions.explanation: ⚠️ Digoxin should only be used after echocardiographic confirmation of the defect and cardiac function. Deducted −15 pts.
⚠️ NSAIDs cause fluid retention and worsen cardiac failure. Avoid in infants with heart failure. Deducted −15 pts.

hpc_onset.text: (Mother) Since about 4–6 weeks of age he has been breathing very fast especially during feeds. He sweats on his forehead when feeding. Feeds take a very long time — he's exhausted after each feed.
hpc_onset.label: Onset of symptoms

feeding_history.text: (Mother) He takes 2 months to finish a feed that should take 20 minutes. He falls asleep after a few minutes of sucking — too tired to continue. He's not gaining weight well.
feeding_history.label: Feeding difficulty

birth_history.text: (Mother) Born at 38 weeks by SVD. Birth weight 3.4 kg. The paediatrician heard a murmur at birth but said we should wait and see. We were never referred.
birth_history.label: Birth / murmur history

pmh_general.text: (Mother) He had 2 chest infections in the last 4 months. Currently on antibiotics for the second one. Growing slowly — paediatrician said he's below the 3rd centile for weight.
pmh_general.label: Recurrent infections / FTT

fhx_general.text: (Mother) No family history of congenital heart disease. No consanguinity. Normal pregnancy, no diabetes or rubella.
fhx_general.label: Family history / antenatal

exam_general.text: General: Tachypnoeic at rest. RR 54/min ↑↑. HR 162 bpm. Temp 37.2°C. SpO₂ 94% on air. Weight: 4.8 kg (birth weight 3.4 kg — poor gain for 4 months). Sweating. Hepatomegaly — liver 4cm. No cyanosis.
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_cardiovascular.text:
CVS:
• Apex beat: displaced — 5th ICS, mid-axillary line (cardiomegaly)
• Thrill: systolic thrill at lower left sternal border
• HS: loud pansystolic murmur at LLSB (grade 4/6), radiating across precordium
→ Classic VSD murmur. Loud = large defect with significant shunting.
exam_cardiovascular.label: Cardiovascular examination

ix_echo.text:
Echocardiogram:
• Large perimembranous VSD — 10mm diameter
• Left-to-right shunt (Qp:Qs = 3.2:1 — significant)
• LA and LV dilated (volume overload)
• PA pressure elevated (RVSP 52 mmHg)
→ Surgical closure indicated. Refer to cardiac surgery.
ix_echo.label: Echocardiogram

ix_cxr.text:
CXR:
• Cardiomegaly (CTR 0.62)
• Increased pulmonary vascular markings (plethora)
• No consolidation
→ Classic large left-to-right shunt appearance.
ix_cxr.label: CXR

cases.presentingComplaint: Diarrhoea 8 times and vomiting 4 times in the last 24 hours

trapActions.explanation: ⚠️ Antibiotics are NOT routinely indicated for watery diarrhoea in children — most is viral. ORS is the treatment. Deducted −10 pts.
⛔ Antidiarrhoeals (loperamide, lomotil) are CONTRAINDICATED in children under 12 — risk of paralytic ileus and death. Deducted −20 pts.
⚠️ IV fluids are not first-line for mild-moderate dehydration. Oral rehydration solution (ORS) is the WHO/IMCI recommended approach. Deducted −10 pts.

hpc_onset.text: (Mother) Diarrhoea started yesterday morning — watery, no blood. He's passed stool 8 times. He vomited 4 times — now just small amounts. Fever started last night.
hpc_onset.label: Onset

hpc_character.text: (Mother) The stool is watery and yellow — no blood, no mucus. Large amounts each time. He's been crying a lot — seems uncomfortable in his tummy.
hpc_character.label: Stool description

sr_urine.text: (Mother) He's barely passed any urine today — I've only changed one wet nappy since this morning and it was very small and dark.
sr_urine.label: Urine output

feeding_history.text: (Mother) He's refusing food. He takes a few sips of water but vomits after. I haven't given ORS yet — I didn't know I should.
feeding_history.label: Oral intake

sr_fever.text: (Mother) Fever last night — 38.3°C. It's still present. I gave paracetamol syrup.
sr_fever.label: Fever

shx_general.text: (Mother) My older child had diarrhoea last week and recovered. We use tap water — I don't always boil it for the baby.
shx_general.label: Contact / water history

exam_general.text: General: Irritable, crying. Temp 38.4°C. HR 148 bpm ↑. RR 36/min. Sunken eyes ++ (moderate dehydration). Sunken fontanelle. Dry mouth and tongue. Skin pinch: goes back slowly (2–3 seconds) → MODERATE dehydration (WHO IMCI Plan B).
exam_general.label: General — dehydration assessment

exam_abdomen.text: Abdomen: Soft. Mild diffuse tenderness. Hyperactive bowel sounds. No organomegaly. No guarding.
exam_abdomen.label: Abdominal examination

ix_glucose.text:
Blood glucose: 3.4 mmol/L (borderline — monitor)
Electrolytes (if available):
• Na: 134 mmol/L
• K: 3.2 mmol/L ↓
→ Plan B ORS: 75 ml/kg over 4 hours + zinc 10mg daily for 10 days + continued feeding
ix_glucose.label: Glucose / electrolytes

cases.presentingComplaint: 3-week history of gradual onset fever, headache and behaviour change

trapActions.explanation: ⚠️ Fluoroquinolone monotherapy is not appropriate for TBM. Standard HRZE regimen + dexamethasone is required. Deducted −15 pts.
⚠️ Dexamethasone reduces mortality and disability in TBM — it is recommended in all cases for the first 4 weeks. Deducted −15 pts.

hpc_onset.text: (Mother) She's been unwell for 3 weeks — it started slowly. Fever that comes and goes, headache, she stopped eating well. Last week she became confused and stopped playing with her siblings.
hpc_onset.label: Gradual onset

hpc_character.text: (Mother) She has severe headache — she holds her head and cries. Neck has become stiff this week. She's vomited 3 times today. Light seems to hurt her eyes.
hpc_character.label: Meningism features

tb_contact.text: (Mother) Yes — her grandfather has been coughing for months. He lost a lot of weight. He lives with us. He was tested — positive TB. He started treatment 1 month ago.
tb_contact.label: TB contact

sr_weight_loss.text: (Mother) She's lost weight over these 3 weeks. She has no appetite. She looks thinner. I noticed a small swelling in her neck 2 weeks ago.
sr_weight_loss.label: Constitutional symptoms

immunisation.text: (Mother) She received BCG at birth — there's a scar on her left arm. But BCG doesn't fully protect against TBM, I was told.
immunisation.label: BCG status

pmh_general.text: (Mother) No previous illnesses. No HIV diagnosis. Not on any medications.
pmh_general.label: Past medical history

exam_general.text: General: Ill, drowsy. GCS 12/15. Temp 38.4°C. HR 112 bpm. RR 28/min. BP 96/60. Wasted appearance. Lymphadenopathy: cervical nodes — firm, matted, 2–3 nodes right side. No hepatosplenomegaly.
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_neuro.text: Neuro: GCS 12. Neck rigidity (Brudzinski +). Kernig's sign: positive. Cranial nerve VI palsy (right lateral rectus weakness — false localising sign of raised ICP). No papilloedema. Fundoscopy: choroidal tubercles visible (pathognomonic of miliary TB).
exam_neuro.label: Neurological examination

ix_csf.text:
CSF (after CT head — no herniation):
• Appearance: clear/xanthochromic
• Cells: 240/μL — predominantly lymphocytes (85%)
• Protein: 2.8 g/L ↑↑ (markedly raised)
• Glucose: 1.2 mmol/L ↓↓ (CSF:blood ratio 0.3)
• AFB smear: positive (rare but specific)
• CBNAAT/GeneXpert: Mycobacterium tuberculosis detected
→ TBM confirmed.
ix_csf.label: CSF analysis

ix_cxr.text:
CXR: Miliary pattern — diffuse bilateral micronodular opacities (1–3mm)
→ Miliary TB with TBM. Mandelbrot staging: Stage II (GCS 12, no focal deficit other than CN VI).
ix_cxr.label: CXR — miliary pattern

cases.presentingComplaint: Rash on the legs, joint pains and abdominal pain for 5 days

trapActions.explanation: ⚠️ HSP is autoimmune — antibiotics are only indicated if an active infection is identified. Deducted −10 pts.
⛔ Aspirin is contraindicated in children — Reye's syndrome risk. Deducted −20 pts.

hpc_onset.text: (Mother) She had a throat infection 2 weeks ago — it settled with rest. Then 5 days ago she developed this rash on her legs. Joint pains started next day, and stomach pain the day after.
hpc_onset.label: Onset / preceding infection

sr_rash.text: (Mother) The rash is mainly on both legs — bottom half. Some on the buttocks. They're raised, purple-red spots that don't go away when I press them. Not itchy.
sr_rash.label: Rash description

sr_joints.text: My knees and ankles hurt — both sides. They're a little swollen. I can still walk but it hurts. My wrists hurt a little too.
sr_joints.label: Joint symptoms

sr_abdomen.text: Yes, I've had tummy pain — crampy, comes and goes. I vomited once. No blood in my stool that I've seen.
sr_abdomen.label: Abdominal pain

sr_urine.text: (Mother) Her urine looked slightly pink-brown yesterday. Today it looks more normal.
sr_urine.label: Urine / renal involvement

pmh_general.text: (Mother) No previous similar illness. No known allergies. Normal development.
pmh_general.label: Past medical history

exam_general.text: General: Well, walking (with mild limp). Temp 37.3°C. HR 94 bpm. BP 104/68 (normal for age — monitor closely for hypertension in HSP). RR 22/min. SpO₂ 99%.
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_skin.text: Skin: Symmetrical palpable purpura — predominantly on extensor surfaces of both legs and buttocks. Non-blanching. Most lesions 2–8mm. Some ecchymotic patches. Distribution classic for HSP.
exam_skin.label: Skin examination

exam_joints.text: Joints: Bilateral ankle and knee swelling — warm, tender. Full ROM preserved. No joint effusion. Wrists: mild tenderness.
exam_joints.label: Joint examination

ix_urinalysis.text:
Urinalysis:
• Blood: 2+ (haematuria)
• Protein: 1+ (proteinuria)
→ Renal involvement present — HSP nephritis. Monitor BP and renal function closely.
→ Renal biopsy if nephrotic or nephritic syndrome develops.
ix_urinalysis.label: Urinalysis — renal involvement

ix_fbc.text:
FBC:
• WBC: 11.4 × 10⁹/L (mild elevation)
• Platelets: 340 × 10⁹/L (NORMAL — differentiates from ITP)
• CRP: 44 mg/L ↑ (mild)
→ Normal platelets exclude ITP. Diagnosis is clinical.
ix_fbc.label: FBC / platelets

cases.presentingComplaint: Projectile vomiting after every feed for 10 days

trapActions.explanation: ⚠️ PPIs treat GORD, not pyloric stenosis. The treatment for HPS is Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy. Deducted −10 pts.
⚠️ Changing formula does not treat pyloric stenosis. Surgical correction is required. Deducted −10 pts.

hpc_onset.text: (Mother) He was feeding well for the first 3 weeks. Then 10 days ago the vomiting started — it's getting progressively worse. Now it happens after every single feed.
hpc_onset.label: Onset — progressive

hpc_character.text: (Mother) The vomiting is very forceful — it shoots across the room, sometimes 1–2 feet away. It's not dribbling — it's projected. The vomit looks like curdled milk — never green.
hpc_character.label: Projectile, non-bilious

feeding_history.text: (Mother) After he vomits he acts very hungry immediately — he roots and wants to feed again straight away. He's clearly not getting enough.
feeding_history.label: Hungry after vomiting

sr_weight.text: (Mother) He was 3.5 kg at birth. At the 2-week visit he was 4.1 kg. But he hasn't gained since. He looks thinner to me now.
sr_weight.label: Weight concern

sr_stool.text: (Mother) He's been passing much less stool — used to pass stool after every feed, now just once a day. Small amounts.
sr_stool.label: Reduced stool

fhx_general.text: (Mother) My husband was treated for pyloric stenosis as a baby — he had surgery. We didn't know it could recur in our child.
fhx_general.label: Family history

exam_general.text: General: Hungry-looking, alert. Weight 3.8 kg (below birth weight — weight loss). Mild dehydration — sunken fontanelle, dry lips. Jaundice: mild (unconjugated — 'jaundice of pyloric stenosis').
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_abdomen.text:
Abdomen: Flat. Visible peristaltic waves: left-to-right visible waves across upper abdomen after feeding.
Test feed: Olive-shaped, firm mass palpable in epigastrium/RUQ during test feed.
→ PYLORIC OLIVE = pathognomonic of HPS.
exam_abdomen.label: Abdominal examination

ix_ultrasound.text:
Abdominal USS (Pylorus):
• Pyloric muscle thickness: 5mm (>4mm = abnormal)
• Pyloric canal length: 20mm (>16mm = abnormal)
→ Confirms hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Surgical referral for Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy.
ix_ultrasound.label: Pyloric USS

ix_lft.text:
Electrolytes:
• Na: 132 mmol/L ↓
• K: 2.8 mmol/L ↓↓
• Cl: 88 mmol/L ↓↓
• HCO₃: 32 mmol/L ↑
• pH: 7.52 (alkalosis)
→ Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis — CLASSIC electrolyte pattern of HPS. Correct before surgery.
ix_lft.label: Electrolytes — classic pattern

cases.presentingComplaint: Bowed legs noticed since the child started walking at 14 months

trapActions.explanation: ⚠️ Rickets is caused by Vitamin D and/or calcium deficiency — not Vitamin A. Deducted −10 pts.
⚠️ Surgical correction should only be considered for persistent deformity after medical treatment and radiological assessment. Deducted −15 pts.

hpc_onset.text: (Mother) His legs have been bowed since he started walking at 14 months. He walks with a waddling gait. They've not gotten better — if anything slightly worse.
hpc_onset.label: Onset

feeding_history.text: (Mother) He was breastfed exclusively for 12 months but without any vitamin D supplement. Now he eats mostly pap and rice — little meat or fish. We don't give him milk or dairy products.
feeding_history.label: Dietary history

sun_exposure.text: (Mother) In our community, we keep babies indoors — we believe direct sunlight is harmful to babies. He's rarely outside. He's always fully covered.
sun_exposure.label: Sun exposure

sr_seizures.text: (Mother) He had one seizure at 8 months — the doctor said it might have been caused by low calcium. He was given calcium treatment then.
sr_seizures.label: Hypocalcaemic seizure

pmh_general.text: (Mother) He had a seizure at 8 months. No other illnesses. Development: walking (though late — at 14 months). Speech normal.
pmh_general.label: Past medical history

exam_general.text: General: Alert, well-nourished appearing. Height: 82 cm (50th centile). Weight: 11.4 kg. Head: frontal bossing present. Fontanelle: closed. Teeth: delayed eruption (only 8 teeth at 24 months — expected 16).
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_msk.text:
Musculoskeletal:
• Genu varum (bow legs) bilaterally — intercondylar distance 8cm
• Rachitic rosary: palpable nodular enlargement at costochondral junctions
• Widening of wrists (metaphyseal widening)
• Harrison's sulcus (groove along lower chest wall)
→ Classic nutritional rickets signs.
exam_msk.label: Bone deformities

ix_xray.text:
Wrist X-ray:
• Cupping, fraying and splaying of metaphyses (distal radius/ulna)
• Widened growth plate
• Reduced bone density (osteopaenia)
→ Classic radiological rickets.
ix_xray.label: Wrist X-ray

ix_calcium.text:
Biochemistry:
• Serum calcium: 1.8 mmol/L ↓ (hypocalcaemia)
• Phosphate: 0.7 mmol/L ↓↓
• ALP: 680 IU/L ↑↑↑ (markedly raised — osteoblast activity)
• 25-OH Vitamin D: 12 nmol/L ↓↓ (deficient — <50 nmol/L)
• PTH: 186 pg/mL ↑ (secondary hyperparathyroidism)
ix_calcium.label: Calcium / Vitamin D

cases.presentingComplaint: Shortness of breath, joint pains and recent sore throat — now with heart murmur

trapActions.explanation: ⚠️ In ARF with significant carditis, use aspirin (children > 12y) or naproxen — NOT ibuprofen as first-line. In this child, aspirin is borderline; naproxen is safer. Deducted −15 pts.
⛔ Secondary prophylaxis with monthly benzathine penicillin is MANDATORY in ARF to prevent recurrence and progressive valve damage. Minimum 10 years or until age 25. Deducted −20 pts.

hpc_onset.text: I had a very sore throat about 3 weeks ago — I took some tablets from the pharmacy but didn't complete the course. About 1 week later my joints started to hurt.
hpc_onset.label: Preceding sore throat

sr_joints.text: My knees, ankles and wrists have been very painful and swollen — it moves from joint to joint. The right knee was worst on Monday, now the left ankle is worst today. It's very painful, warm and swollen.
sr_joints.label: Migratory polyarthritis

sr_chest.text: I've been getting short of breath when I climb stairs. Sometimes I hear my own heartbeat very fast at rest. I feel chest tightness sometimes.
sr_chest.label: Cardiac symptoms

sr_skin.text: My mum noticed a pink ring-shaped rash on my body last week — it was faint and not itchy. It seems to have faded now.
sr_skin.label: Erythema marginatum

sr_neuro.text: My teacher said I've been making sudden jerky movements I don't seem to control — especially my hands. My handwriting has gotten worse.
sr_neuro.label: Sydenham's chorea

pmh_general.text: I had a similar sore throat 6 months ago. No previous diagnosis of rheumatic fever. No known heart disease.
pmh_general.label: Recurrent strep history

exam_general.text: General: Ill-looking, febrile. Temp 38.8°C. HR 118 bpm. BP 100/64. RR 24/min. Involuntary purposeless movements of hands noted (chorea). Faint annular erythematous rash on trunk.
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_cardiovascular.text:
CVS:
• Apex beat: displaced (cardiomegaly)
• HS I + II + soft S3
• Pansystolic murmur at apex (MR) grade 3/6, radiating to axilla
• Mid-diastolic murmur at apex (Carey Coombs murmur — mitral valvulitis)
→ Carditis: 2 murmurs + displaced apex = significant carditis.
exam_cardiovascular.label: Cardiovascular examination

ix_echo.text:
Echocardiogram:
• Mitral regurgitation — moderate (RHD in evolution)
• Aortic valve: minimal regurgitation
• LA and LV mildly dilated
• Pericardial effusion: trivial
→ Confirms carditis. Jones Criteria met: 2 major (carditis + migratory polyarthritis) + 1 minor (fever) + evidence of strep infection.
ix_echo.label: Echocardiogram

ix_culture.text:
Throat swab: Group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus (GAS) isolated
ASO titre: 640 IU/mL ↑↑ (>200 = significant — confirms recent strep infection)
CRP: 112 mg/L ↑. ESR: 78 mm/hr ↑
ECG: prolonged PR interval (0.24 sec) — 1st degree AV block (minor criterion)
ix_culture.label: Strep evidence / bloods

cases.presentingComplaint: Perianal itching at night, abdominal pain and poor sleep for 3 weeks

trapActions.explanation: ⚠️ Mebendazole is not recommended for children under 1 year of age. This child is 5 years old — it is appropriate here. Deducted −10 pts.

hpc_onset.text: (Mother) About 3 weeks ago she started complaining that her bottom itches at night. She can't sleep well. She scratches herself and is irritable in the mornings.
hpc_onset.label: Onset

hpc_character.text: (Mother) The itching is specifically at night — during the day she seems fine. She's also had tummy ache — crampy, around the belly button. Her appetite has reduced.
hpc_character.label: Nocturnal pruritus

sr_worms.text: (Mother) Yes — I saw tiny white worms on her bottom at night when I checked. They were very small, thin and white — moving.
sr_worms.label: Worms seen

shx_general.text: (Mother) She goes to nursery school. She plays in the compound — often with soil. Her hygiene isn't always perfect — she doesn't always wash hands before eating.
shx_general.label: Hygiene / school exposure

fhx_general.text: (Mother) Her younger brother (age 3) has also been scratching his bottom recently. Father hasn't complained.
fhx_general.label: Household contacts

pmh_general.text: (Mother) She's been healthy. No hospital admissions. Fully vaccinated. She was dewormed once at age 2 with a single-dose tablet.
pmh_general.label: Past deworming

exam_general.text: General: Well, alert, cooperative. Normal vital signs. Temp 36.8°C. Slightly pale (mild anaemia). No jaundice. Weight: 18 kg (appropriate for age).
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_abdomen.text:
Abdomen: Soft. Mild periumbilical tenderness. No organomegaly. Bowel sounds normal.
Perianal: erythema and excoriation around anus — scratch marks visible.
exam_abdomen.label: Abdominal / perianal examination

ix_tape_test.text:
Sellotape/tape test (perianal swab at night or first thing in morning):
→ Enterobius vermicularis eggs identified on microscopy.
Stool O&P: Enterobius eggs found
→ Confirms threadworm (pinworm) infestation.
ix_tape_test.label: Tape test / stool O&P

ix_fbc.text:
FBC:
• Hb: 10.8 g/dL (mild anaemia)
• Eosinophils: 0.9 × 10⁹/L ↑ (eosinophilia — worm infestation)
→ Treat patient AND household contacts. Treat twice 2 weeks apart to catch newly hatched worms.
ix_fbc.label: FBC

cases.presentingComplaint: Jitteriness and poor feeding in a macrosomic neonate born to a diabetic mother

trapActions.explanation: ⛔ NEVER give insulin to a hypoglycaemic neonate — this is an absolute contraindication that could be fatal. Treat with dextrose. Deducted −25 pts.
⚠️ Jitteriness in a high-risk neonate (IDM) requires immediate blood glucose check. Do not observe without checking. Deducted −15 pts.

birth_history.text: (Mother) She was born 2 hours ago by caesarean section at 38 weeks. Birth weight 4.6 kg — the doctor said she's large for dates. APGAR was 7 and 9.
birth_history.label: Birth history / macrosomia

maternal_history.text: (Mother) I have gestational diabetes — diagnosed at 28 weeks. My blood sugars were not well controlled despite diet changes. I was started on metformin at 32 weeks.
maternal_history.label: Maternal diabetes

hpc_character.text: (Nurse) Baby has been jittery since 90 minutes of age — fine tremor of hands and chin. She's been difficult to rouse for feeding. One episode of eye deviation noticed.
hpc_character.label: Jitteriness / symptoms

feeding_history.text: (Mother) We tried breastfeeding immediately after birth as instructed but she's too sleepy to latch. She hasn't fed properly yet.
feeding_history.label: Feeding attempts

pmh_general.text: (Mother) No previous pregnancy complications. This is my first child. No family history of diabetes.
pmh_general.label: Obstetric history

exam_general.text: General: Macrosomic infant (4.6 kg). Jittery — fine tremor hands and chin. Plethoric (ruddy) complexion. Mild hypotonia. Temp 36.5°C. HR 164 bpm. RR 56/min. SpO₂ 97%.
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_neuro.text: Neuro: Jitteriness stops when limb is held passively (differentiates from seizure). Moro reflex: weak. Suck reflex: poor. Tone: mildly reduced. No focal deficit.
exam_neuro.label: Neurological examination

ix_glucose.text:
Bedside blood glucose: 1.6 mmol/L ↓↓ (symptomatic hypoglycaemia — threshold for treatment: <2.6 mmol/L in neonates)
→ Symptomatic: IV 10% dextrose 2ml/kg bolus STAT
→ Then 10% dextrose infusion at glucose infusion rate (GIR) 6–8 mg/kg/min
→ Recheck glucose in 30 minutes
ix_glucose.label: Blood glucose — urgent

ix_fbc.text:
FBC:
• Hb: 22.4 g/dL ↑ (polycythaemia — common in IDM)
• WBC: 13.8 × 10⁹/L (normal)
• Haematocrit: 67% ↑ (polycythaemia — increases viscosity, risk of NEC)
Serum calcium: 1.82 mmol/L ↓ (hypocalcaemia — also common in IDM)
→ IDM complications: hypoglycaemia, polycythaemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia
ix_fbc.label: FBC / calcium

cases.presentingComplaint: Rash covering the whole body, high fever and red eyes for 4 days

trapActions.explanation: ⚠️ Antibiotics are not indicated for uncomplicated measles — it's viral. Only for secondary bacterial complications (pneumonia, otitis media). Deducted −10 pts.
⚠️ There is no specific antiviral for measles. Treatment is supportive + Vitamin A. Deducted −10 pts.

hpc_onset.text: (Mother) He had high fever, runny nose and red eyes for 3 days. On day 4 the rash appeared — it started on his face and spread downward to his body, arms and legs.
hpc_onset.label: Onset — prodrome then rash

sr_rash.text: (Mother) The rash is red — flat and bumpy spots that are joining together. Started behind his ears and on the face, then spread down. His whole body is covered now.
sr_rash.label: Rash description — morbilliform

sr_fever.text: (Mother) Very high fever — 40°C. It actually increased when the rash appeared. He's very miserable.
sr_fever.label: Fever

immunisation.text: (Mother) He missed his 9-month measles vaccine. We were away and then forgot. He never got it.
immunisation.label: Vaccination status

sr_eyes.text: (Mother) Yes — both eyes are very red and discharging — yellow crusting every morning. They seem sensitive to light. I keep wiping them.
sr_eyes.label: Conjunctivitis / photophobia

hpc_character.text: (Mother) Runny nose, barking cough and very red eyes started first — 3 days before the rash. The cough is worsening.
hpc_character.label: 3 C's — coryza, cough, conjunctivitis

shx_general.text: (Mother) His classmate at nursery school had similar rash last week. We live in a densely populated area.
shx_general.label: Contact history

exam_general.text: General: Ill, miserable, crying. Temp 40.1°C. HR 138 bpm. RR 42/min. SpO₂ 95%. Bilateral conjunctival injection + mucopurulent discharge. Koplik's spots: white spots on buccal mucosa (PATHOGNOMONIC of measles).
exam_general.label: General — Koplik's spots

exam_skin.text:
Skin: Maculopapular rash covering face, trunk, limbs — coalescing on the face. Rash blanches on pressure. Spreads cephalocaudally.
→ Classic measles rash distribution.
exam_skin.label: Skin examination

ix_fbc.text:
FBC:
• WBC: 3.8 × 10⁹/L ↓ (leucopaenia — typical of viral measles)
• Lymphocytes: 1.2 × 10⁹/L ↓
→ Measles causes lymphopaenia — immunosuppression lasting up to 2–3 years (immune amnesia)
→ Vitamin A: 2 doses of 200,000 IU (age 3) reduces severity and mortality
ix_fbc.label: FBC / treatment

cases.presentingComplaint: Delayed walking, stiff legs and feeding difficulties since infancy

trapActions.explanation: ⚠️ Brain MRI is indicated in all children with CP to define the aetiology and guide prognosis. Deducted −10 pts.

birth_history.text: (Mother) She was born at 30 weeks — premature. She spent 6 weeks in the NICU. She needed a ventilator for 2 weeks. She had a brain scan in hospital that showed some white matter changes.
birth_history.label: Prematurity / NICU

hpc_onset.text: (Mother) From about 4 months I noticed she held her legs very stiff when I dressed her. She couldn't sit by 9 months. She's 2 now and still not walking. She bottom-shuffles.
hpc_onset.label: Motor delay

feeding_history.text: (Mother) She has always had trouble feeding — poor suck, gagging on solids. She drools a lot. Feeding takes over an hour each time.
feeding_history.label: Feeding/oromotor difficulties

dev_history.text: (Mother) Smiling: 3 months (late). Sitting: not achieved. Standing with support: just started. No walking. Speech: 5 single words — she mostly babbles. She understands commands.
dev_history.label: Developmental milestones

sr_seizures.text: (Mother) She had 3 seizures between 6 and 12 months — the neurologist started her on sodium valproate. She's been seizure-free for 8 months now.
sr_seizures.label: Seizure history

fhx_general.text: (Mother) No family history of neurological conditions. I'm 28 years old. Normal pregnancy — premature labour was spontaneous.
fhx_general.label: Family history

exam_general.text: General: Alert, interactive, friendly. Small for age. Head circumference: 44cm (below 3rd centile — microcephaly). Cannot stand independently.
exam_general.label: General examination

exam_neuro.text:
Neuro:
• Tone: increased bilaterally in lower limbs (spasticity) — 'clasp-knife' rigidity
• Reflexes: brisk bilaterally, sustained clonus at ankles
• Plantars: extensor (upgoing)
• Upper limbs: mildly increased tone
• Gait: scissoring (when supported)
• Cranial nerves: intact
→ Upper motor neurone pattern — consistent with spastic diplegia.
exam_neuro.label: Neurological examination

ix_mri.text:
MRI Brain:
• Periventricular leukomalacia (PVL) — white matter loss around ventricles
• Cystic changes in bilateral periventricular white matter
• Mild ventriculomegaly
→ PVL is the most common MRI finding in premature infants with spastic diplegia CP.
ix_mri.label: MRI brain
